g.text: The average of the last W — stack and heap at every step
9 values, W = 3 · 21 reads vs 15 operations · 2 answers withheld · 6 of 7 drift with one value at 10000000000000000
2 // primitive: VALUES — what arrives, in order. Written index:value.
4 // primitive: W = 3 — how many of the most recent to average.
5 // primitive: sum — the running total of the window. One number, not a list.
7 // primitive: NOT_YET — fewer than W values have arrived, so there is no answer.
8 // primitive: HUGE = 10000000000000000 — one value replaced by a large one, so the window holds a
9 // mixture of magnitudes. Scaling every value equally does NOT drift; the mixture does.
10 // primitive: allWindows(f) — run f over every window in turn, for comparison.
12 // primitive: runningAnswer(i) / recomputedAnswer(i) — the two methods' i-th answers.
16 // "Values arrive one at a time, forever. Report the average of the last W after every
17 // arrival. You may not re-read the window. Then: what do you report before W values
18 // have arrived? Then: is the running total exactly right?"
20 // function: recomputeAt(xs, i) — the answer everyone gives first: add up the window.
32 // function: onArrival(xs, i) — add what came in, subtract what left. Two operations,
35 // 9 additions and 6 subtractions in all, against 21 reads
43 // function: report(i) — the answer, or NOT_YET. The guard is the one everyone forgets.
50 // function: driftAt(i) — how far the running total has wandered from the truth, at a
51 // magnitude where a double cannot hold both the total and one value.
57 // function: main() — both answers, the warm-up, then the drift.
60 val fast = allWindows(report) // 15 operations, same answers
62 val same = true // exact on these values
63 val drift = 6 // of 7 answers, with one value at 10000000000000000
Step 1/0 — 9 values, a window of 3, an answer per arrival
0x100 holds 0:5 1:3 2:7 3:2 4:6 5:1 6:9 7:4 8:8 and 0x200 is the only state the fast answer will need: **one number**. "Forever" is the constraint — the stream
does not end, so nothing can be held that grows with the arrivals.

Step 2/0 — the first answer: add up the window
3 reads give 5 for the first window. Correct, and 7 windows × 3 = 21 reads here — at W = 10⁵ it is 10⁵ reads **per arrival**, so the cost is set by the window size when

Step 3/0 — the reframe: one number, two operations
The window's total is kept rather than its contents. Adding the arrival is half of it; the other half is noticing that **exactly one value leaves** when one arrives, so
the update is a constant two operations whatever W is.

At arrival 3, index 0 is now outside the window, so its value 5 is subtracted: sum becomes 12. Note what this needs — **the departing value**, which means the last W
values must still be reachable even though only the total is being maintained. The "one number" claim is about the total, not about the memory.

Step 5/0 — and before 3 have arrived there is no answer
After 2 arrivals the total is 8, and dividing by 3 would report 2.67 — an average of 3 values when only 2 exist. **2 answers are withheld**, which is W − 1, and the
usual bug is to divide by W from the first arrival and quietly report a figure that is too low for the first 2 of them.

Step 7/0 — so is the running total exactly right?
On these values, yes — asserted answer by answer. That is worth checking rather than assuming, because the two methods are not the same computation: one adds 3 numbers
from scratch, the other adds and subtracts 15 times. They agree here because the values are small integers.

Step 8/0 — now one value replaced by 10000000000000000
Replace one value with 10000000000000000 and the two methods **stop agreeing**: 6 of 7 answers differ, the worst by 0.666666666666667. The reason is that a double cannot
hold the total and one value to the same precision, so **adding a value and later subtracting it does not return to where you started** — each window's total carries the
residue of every value that has ever passed through it.

Step 9/0 — and the error only accumulates
There is no step that corrects it: the total is never recomputed, so a residue introduced at arrival 3 is still in the total at arrival a million. Recomputation has no
such problem and costs W reads. **The fast answer trades exactness for a cost independent of W**, and whether that trade is acceptable depends on the magnitudes — which
is a property of the data, not of the algorithm.

Step 10/0 — which is why integers are worth insisting on
Integer addition and subtraction are exact and reversible, so the drift disappears entirely — which is why money is counted in pence and latencies in microseconds rather
than as fractions. If the values must be fractional, the fix is to recompute periodically, which bounds the residue to whatever accumulates between recomputations.

Step 11/0 — and what else the window needs
The subtraction reads index 0, so the last W values must be retained — a ring buffer of W entries, not the whole stream. So the real cost is O(1) **time** and O(W)
**space**, and claiming O(1) for both is the overstatement to avoid: the total is one number and the window is still W values.

Two operations per arrival instead of 3, W values retained, and 2 answers withheld at the start. Three things to volunteer: the warm-up is **W − 1 answers**, not a
rounding detail; the space is **O(W)** even though the time is O(1); and the running total is **exact only for exact arithmetic** — 6 of 7 answers drift as soon as one
value is large enough to swamp the others, and no step ever corrects it.
